strengths: Well-motivated practical problem with clear demonstration of efficiency-accuracy trade-off (Figure 1)
Technically sound approach with good motivation from L2 concentration observation (Appendix C.1) and elegant per-layer dimensionality reduction strategy
Comprehensive empirical evaluation across multiple models (1.5B-7B), datasets (GLUE, C4), and proper baselines including strong LQ-LoRA baseline
Strong and consistent empirical results: 2.36%-10.37% accuracy gains over Q-LoRA, 11/12 improvements over Q-LoRA at different ranks, comparable or superior to LQ-LoRA with single training
Thorough ablation studies and analysis of generalization to unseen configurations with good alignment (Figure 7)
Clear presentation with good figures and reproducible details (layer specifications, hyperparameters, algorithmic descriptions)
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: configuration-aware model is straightforward MLP mapping, Pareto-based GP is standard technique, and L2 concentration observation is from prior work (Zhu et al., 2024)

Unfair baseline comparison: Q-LoRA/LQ-LoRA evaluated at only 4 bit-widths while CoA-LoRA evaluated on 50 configurations, creating potential bias in HV improvements; comparison should be at same 4 bit-widths
Misleading computational cost claims: paper claims 'no additional time cost' but Table 2 shows CoA-LoRA (52-91 min) is 2-3× slower than Shared-LoRA (19-35 min); lacks breakdown of time components

Insufficient technical justification: finite-difference δ=1 choice unjustified, configuration embedding details vague, model θ architecture unstated, no comparison with alternative initialization strategies

Limited generalization scope: evaluated only on 1.5B-7B models (not 13B+ where quantization matters most), mixed zero-shot results (Table C.3), SST-2 misalignment unexplained, no analysis of failure modes
Statistical rigor issues: no error bars, confidence intervals, or multiple seeds; modest improvements (2.36% on SST-2) without significance testing
Missing baselines and comparisons: no simple baselines (e.g., interpolation), no other configuration-aware quantization methods, no evaluation on alternative adapter approaches

strengths: Well-motivated practical problem with clear gap between per-configuration fine-tuning (slow) and shared adapters (inaccurate)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple models (RoBERTa, Qwen, LLaMA) and diverse tasks (GLUE, C4)
Solid empirical results showing 2.36%-10.37% improvements over Q-LoRA while reducing training time significantly
Demonstrates generalization to unseen configurations with good alignment (Figure 7)
Includes reasonable ablations on configuration search effectiveness and different LoRA ranks
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core idea of configuration-to-adjustment mapping is straightforward; uses standard techniques (GP-based optimization, Pareto filtering) without conceptual innovation

Critical design choice unjustified: claims 'most adaptation signal in L₂' but Appendix C.1 shows L₂ has very low correlations (0.01-0.16) while L₁ has high correlations (0.78-0.88), suggesting the choice may be inverted; no empirical validation that L₂-only is optimal

Incomplete baseline comparisons: QA-LoRA (cited) never compared; missing comparisons to simpler alternatives (adapter interpolation, meta-learning); limited comparison scope (Q-LoRA/LQ-LoRA shown at 4 bit-widths vs. CoA-LoRA at 50)
Modest improvements lack statistical validation: 2.36%-10.37% gains with no confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests; some improvements within noise margins (e.g., 0.58% on QQP)

Configuration search adds substantial complexity for minimal benefit: Figure 8 shows only ~1-2% improvement, yet introduces multiple hyperparameters (U, δ, T₂) with task-dependent sensitivity (Figure C.2) and unclear guidance on setting

Limited analysis and insights: no visualization of learned adjustments; no failure case analysis; missing generalization tests beyond 2.5-6.25 bit-width training range; minimal interpretability of what θ discovers

Presentation issues: unnecessarily complicated configuration representation (z_i, m_i, b_i embeddings); notation overloading; dense writing; missing computational cost breakdown and ablations isolating component contributions

Reproducibility concerns: no code availability mentioned; hyperparameters scattered across appendices; requires proprietary Gurobi solver; insufficient detail on calibration data and training procedures

strengths: Addresses a practical and well-motivated problem: efficient LoRA adaptation across diverse quantization configurations for heterogeneous edge deployment

Smart technical design with dimensionality reduction: mapping configuration→L2 adjustments (I+Uθ(Ci))L2,i reduces output space significantly while leveraging empirical insight that L2 captures shared knowledge (Fig. C.1)

Principled Pareto-based optimization: sophisticated use of Expected Hypervolume Improvement with Gaussian processes, finite-difference gradient approximation, and diversity-preserving segmented filtering for discrete configuration spaces

Comprehensive experimental validation: multiple model scales (1.5B-7B), diverse datasets (C4+GLUE), strong baselines, thorough ablations (config search, rank sensitivity, segment analysis), and generalization studies

Consistent and strong empirical results: 2.36%-10.37% accuracy gains over Q-LoRA on GLUE with single training run; HV improvements of 3%-8% vs LQ-LoRA; effective generalization to unseen configurations (<1% deviation in most cases)
Well-executed presentation: clear motivation (Fig. 1), effective visualizations (Figs. 2-4), and accessible writing that makes the approach understandable
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: individual components (config embeddings, GP optimization, Pareto filtering) are standard techniques; contribution is primarily in engineering the combination rather than introducing fundamentally new methods

Training cost claims lack clarity: abstract claims 'no additional time cost' but Table 2 shows 50-90 minutes; advantage over Q-LoRA (20-40 min per config) only apparent when serving many configurations; missing breakdown of config search vs. model training overhead

Evaluation fairness concerns: baselines evaluated at only 4 bit-widths (2.5-4) while CoA-LoRA tested at 50+ configurations, creating asymmetry in HV comparison; missing alternative baselines (e.g., uniform interval sampling)

Insufficient analysis of learned representations: no visualization of how Uθ varies across configurations; unclear which Pareto-optimal configs are selected and why; limited sensitivity analysis to initial configuration set

Generalization limitations underexplored: SST-2 shows ~1% generalization gap while other tasks perform better, but no principled analysis of task-dependent factors; generalization only tested within 4-6 bit range
Limited scope: only NormalFloat quantization evaluated; no mixed-precision quantization, very low-bit (<2 bits), or comparison with other multi-config/meta-learning approaches

Hyperparameter sensitivity not thoroughly addressed: segment count U shows task-dependent variation (Fig. C.2); selection of reference points for HV appears arbitrary; guidance on T1, T2, δ settings lacking
Missing implementation details: GP kernel selection not specified; stopping criteria for config search unclear; no discussion of random seed robustness; code availability not mentioned
Incremental task-specific improvements: on MNLI/QQP, gains vs LQ-LoRA are modest (5.95%, 2.68%), raising questions about consistency across different problem types

strengths: Well-motivated practical problem with clear efficiency-accuracy tradeoff (Figure 1)
Efficient architecture design: r×r adjustments reduce output dimensionality significantly (<0.5% parameters)
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple models (1.5B-13B), datasets, and settings with consistent improvements (1.74%-8.89% over baselines)
Strong generalization to unseen configurations with minimal performance degradation (Figure 7)
Solid practical contribution: training time ~1 hour vs 20-40 min per configuration for baselines
Thorough ablations and sensitivity analysis (configuration search impact, rank variations, segment numbers)
Clear presentation with reproducible implementation details
weaknesses: Fairness concern in baseline comparisons: QLoRA/LQ-LoRA evaluated on only 5 configurations while CoA-LoRA uses 50, conflating better configuration selection with better per-configuration adaptation
Limited methodological novelty: configuration-aware model is standard MLP architecture; Gaussian process optimization is well-established; primary contribution is engineering combination
Incomplete analysis of failure modes: SST-2 shows weaker generalization (Figure 7) with insufficient explanation; lower bit-width instability (Table C.5) unexplained
Training cost accounting lacks transparency: claimed 'no additional cost' but comparison baseline unclear (2 vs 50 configurations); time breakdown between search and training not provided
Configuration search design choices unjustified: finite-difference step size δ=1 without ablation; coordinate ascent without comparison to alternatives; weak random extension baseline
Limited scope: method tailored to NormalFloat quantization; untested with other schemes or LoRA variants (AdaLoRA, DoRA); 'unseen configurations' are similar to training set

Theoretical gaps: no analysis of when/why generalization should work; L2 concentration property only empirically justified (Appendix C.1); missing properties of configuration space enabling generalization
Experimental instabilities: zero-shot results show mixed improvements (Table C.3); segment parameter sensitivity is task-dependent (Figure C.3) without principled selection guidance
Missing critical comparisons: no evaluation of baselines on all 50 configurations; no comparison to simpler shared-LoRA variants or meta-learning approaches

strengths: Well-motivated practical problem with clear real-world applicability for deploying quantized LLMs on heterogeneous devices
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple datasets (GLUE, C4), model sizes (1.5B-7B), and settings with thorough ablation studies
Solid engineering design with effective dimensionality reduction via r×r adjustment matrices and efficient per-layer parallelization
Consistent improvements of 1.74%-8.89% over baselines while providing significant time savings compared to per-configuration fine-tuning
Demonstrates good scalability across model sizes with stable performance and analysis of generalization to unseen configurations
weaknesses: Overstated core claims: 'on-the-fly adaptation' requires training on fixed 50 configurations; 'no additional cost' contradicted by Table 2 (57-91 min vs. 20-40 min per config)

Limited technical novelty: combines existing techniques (configuration embedding, MLP mapping, GP-based Pareto optimization, finite-difference gradients) without significant algorithmic or conceptual innovation

Weak generalization analysis: Figure 7 only tests interpolations of seen bit-widths; no principled bounds on generalization error; SST-2 shows 1% discrepancy indicating non-negligible drift for unseen configs

Questionable experimental design: hypervolume metric appears arbitrary; modest configuration search benefit (~2% in Fig. 8); Shared-LoRA sometimes competitive; baselines evaluated at only 5 bit-widths vs. 50 for CoA-LoRA

Insufficient technical justification: 50 configurations without ablation; GP trained on single calibration batch; segment count U=40 appears arbitrary; unclear scalability to higher-dimensional configuration spaces

Misleading presentation: Figure 2 unclear; Algorithm 1 line 7 vague about discrete sampling; core claim about removing per-configuration fine-tuning overstated since representative config set must be identified offline
Limited scope: only NormalFloat quantization tested; no comparison to meta-learning/interpolation baselines; restricted to LLMs; extreme low-bit regimes not thoroughly explored

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem addressing practical challenges of deploying quantized LLMs on heterogeneous devices
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple architectures (RoBERTa, Qwen, LLaMA), tasks (GLUE, C4), and settings with consistent improvements of 1.74%-8.89% over baselines
Thoughtful technical design leveraging the key insight that adaptation is concentrated in L2 matrices, reducing dimensionality and enabling efficient learning
Strong generalization to unseen configurations (Figure 7) with robust performance under aggressive quantization (2.5-bit)
Thorough ablation studies and sensitivity analyses (Figures 8, C.3; Tables 3-5) demonstrating the value of each component
Excellent reproducibility with detailed algorithm description, architectural specifications, and promised code release
Computational efficiency gains: achieves competitive accuracy in ~1 hour vs. 20-40 minutes per configuration for one-to-one fine-tuning baselines
weaknesses: Moderate technical novelty: individual components (MLP-based generation, Gaussian process optimization, Pareto filtering) are relatively standard; novelty lies primarily in problem formulation and integration rather than fundamental innovation

Experimental fairness concerns: CoA-LoRA evaluated on 50 dense configurations while QLoRA/LQ-LoRA only evaluated on 5 discrete points, potentially inflating hypervolume comparisons; fair comparison would use identical configuration sets

Incomplete computational cost analysis: training time reported (~57-91 min) excludes iterative search overhead; total cost vs. N separate fine-tuning runs (N×20-40 min) not clearly quantified for practical deployment scenarios

Limited theoretical justification: why r×r adjustment in L2 is sufficient, and design choices (reparameterization as I+U_θ, d=8, hidden size 128) lack principled motivation; based on empirical observation only

Configuration generalization not fully validated: no analysis of how far out-of-distribution configurations can drift before performance degrades; Figure 7 shows up to 1% misalignment on SST-2; assumption that final set C is representative needs stronger justification

Hyperparameter choices appear arbitrary without proper ablation: embedding dimension, MLP hidden size, finite-difference step size δ=1 (coarse), and U=40 not systematically studied; only U ablated in Figure C.3

Scope limitations: only NormalFloat quantization tested (unclear generalization to RTN, INT schemes); largest model tested is 13B (scalability to much larger models unvalidated); no statistical significance testing or error bars reported

Missing baselines and comparisons: no evaluation against simpler configuration interpolation methods; limited comparison to other parameter generation approaches; unfair sampling density in comparisons

Limited analysis of failure modes and boundary conditions: what happens for extreme configurations far outside training distribution; how does number of training configurations affect performance; no per-configuration head-to-head comparisons
